readerTitle: Who really sets your price: you or the market?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (시장 노점, 청소용품 유통사, 사내 디자인팀) · 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 가격을 정할 힘은 회사 규모가 아니라 고객이 내 상품을 남의 것과 얼마나 다르게 보는지, 얼마나 쉽게 갈아탈 수 있는지에서 나온다. 같은 사업 안에서도 품목마다 가격 수용자이기도 하고 가격 결정자이기도 하다.
misconception: 가격표의 숫자는 내가 쓰니 가격은 내가 정한다. 작은 가게는 늘 시장 가격을 따르고, 큰 회사는 늘 가격을 정한다.

sources.text: 미시경제학의 표준 개념 (가격 수용자와 가격 결정자, 완전경쟁과 시장 지배력)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 6번 카드의 '아주 큰 밀 농장도 시장 가격을 받아들인다'는 교과서의 일반적 설명입니다. 특정 농장이나 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
모든 사례(노점, 유통사의 5% 인하, 사내 디자인팀)는 가상입니다. 해당 카드에 illustrative 표시를 붙였는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Who really sets your price: you or the market?
body: Two stalls at a Saturday market. One sells plain potatoes. When the stall across the aisle drops its price by 20 cents a kilo, she follows within the hour. If she doesn't, her customers walk ten steps.
The other stall sells a smoked chili sauce from a family recipe. He raised the price by a dollar last month. The line didn't get shorter.

image.label: Two market stalls: potatoes and jars of chili sauce
image.brief: 주말 시장 노점 두 곳을 나란히. 왼쪽은 감자 노점, 상인이 건너편 가격표를 보며 자기 가격표를 고쳐 쓰는 모습. 오른쪽은 수제 칠리소스 병이 놓인 노점, 손님 줄이 길게 서 있음. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A big rival cuts prices 5%.
body: You run a distributor that supplies cleaning products to offices and restaurants. Most of your catalog is standard: the same brand-name bleach, gloves and paper towels your rivals carry. A few items are your own blends, mixed to order.
A large rival cuts prices 5% on its standard lines. What do you do?

options.text: Hold all prices. Your customers know and trust you
options.feedback: Trust helps, but on identical boxes buyers compare line by line. You keep your margin and slowly lose the orders.

options.text: Match on the standard lines, keep your prices on the custom blends
options.feedback: You protect volume where customers can switch in one phone call, and keep margin where nobody offers the same thing.

options.text: Match the cut across your whole catalog
options.feedback: It protects every account, but you give away margin on blends where customers weren't comparing prices at all.

cards.title: On some items, you find out your price.
body: On the standard lines, customers see the same product in the same box. Comparing takes a minute and switching takes a call. Your price isn't really yours to choose. You discover it by watching the market.
The custom blends work differently. No rival sells that exact mix, and a customer would have to test a new one before switching. There, you have **room to set the price** yourself.

cards.title: Price takers and price makers
body: A **price taker** has to accept the going market price. Its customers see its offer as the same as others' and can switch easily. Charge more and sales fall away.
A **price maker** has some room to choose its price, because customers see something they can't easily get elsewhere.
Most businesses sit somewhere between the two. The potato stall is near one end. The chili sauce is closer to the other.

image.label: A dial from price taker to price maker
image.brief: 가로 눈금 다이얼 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 끝 "Price taker"에 감자와 표준 표백제 상자, 오른쪽 끝 "Price maker"에 칠리소스 병과 맞춤 세제 통. 바늘이 가운데쯤을 가리킴. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Four things decide where you sit.
body: Your position depends on what customers can see and do, not on what you write on the price tag.
list: **How similar** your offer looks to others'
cards.callout: Notice that company size isn't on the list.
cards.softwareNote: A reseller of generic cloud storage is close to a price taker: buyers compare cost per gigabyte. A small tool built deep into a customer's workflow can be a price maker, because switching means retraining a team and moving data.

cards.title: Size isn't the point.
body: Even a very large wheat farm usually takes the market price. Its wheat looks like everyone else's, and buyers have many sellers.
Meanwhile, a small bakery with a cake people travel for can set its own price.
One business can also be both. A grocery store is close to a price taker on milk and bananas, where shoppers know the prices. It has more room on bread from its own bakery.

image.label: Big farm with a small arrow, small bakery with a big arrow
image.brief: 대비 일러스트. 왼쪽은 넓은 밀밭과 대형 농장, 옆에 작은 화살표와 "Takes the price". 오른쪽은 작은 동네 빵집과 진열된 특별한 케이크, 옆에 큰 화살표와 "Sets the price". 로고 없음.

cards.title: Pricing room has edges.
body: Even a price maker's room is limited. Raise the chili sauce price far enough and customers will try a rival's jar or skip it. Room to set a price is never unlimited.
The opposite mistake costs just as much. Acting like a price maker on a product customers see as identical loses volume quietly.
And being a price taker isn't a failure. It means the game is lower costs and better service, not a higher price.

cards.title: Now it's an in-house design team.
body: You lead the design team inside a large company. Finance now wants you to charge other departments for your work, and they're free to hire outside agencies.
Most requests are standard: banners and slide templates that agencies sell at well-known rates. Some are product launches that need deep brand knowledge and strict secrecy. How do you set your rates?

options.text: One rate for everything, set to cover your team's costs
options.feedback: Simple, but if your rate is above agency prices on standard work, departments will compare and take that work outside.

options.text: Match agency rates on standard work, charge more for launch work
options.feedback: You stay competitive where you're one of many options, and you're paid fairly where outsiders can't easily do the job.

options.text: Price everything below agencies to keep all the work
options.feedback: You keep the volume, but you may not cover your costs, and you underprice the launch work only you can do well.

cards.title: Know where you take the price and where you make it.
body: Where customers see you as the same as others, the market sets your price, so compete on cost. Where they see something they can't get elsewhere, you have room to choose.
**Try it today:** list your top five products or services. Mark each one *taker* or *maker*. Are you pricing each one the way its mark suggests?
